add.title: Social Changes under British Rule – Laws, New Classes, Caste and Women
add.md:
# Social Changes under British Rule
- **Rule of law:** **Indian Penal Code (1860)**, drafted by the First Law Commission under **Macaulay**, and the Civil/Criminal Procedure Codes applied **one law to all castes**
  - Brahmins lost the special privileges in punishment they had under the older Hindu rules
- **Social legislation in sequence:**
  - **Female infanticide** banned (Bengal Regulations 1795, 1804); **Female Infanticide Prevention Act, 1870**
  - **Sati abolished**, Regulation XVII, **1829** (Bentinck)
  - **Slavery abolished**, Act V of **1843** (Ellenborough)
  - **Caste Disabilities Removal Act, 1850**: a convert kept his property rights
  - **Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act, 1856** (Vidyasagar)
  - **Native Marriage Act, 1872** (Brahmo marriage, Keshab Chandra Sen): inter-caste marriage allowed, child marriage barred
  - **Age of Consent Act, 1891**: age of consent raised from 10 to **12** (Malabari, Rakhmabai case)
  - **Sarda Act, 1929** (Child Marriage Restraint): girls **14**, boys **18**
  - **Hindu Women's Right to Property Act, 1937**
- **New social classes:** an English-educated **middle class** (lawyers, teachers, clerks, journalists) that later led reform and the national movement
  - New **zamindars and moneylenders** under the land settlements; tenants and agricultural labourers grew; craftsmen were ruined by **deindustrialisation**
  - A small **industrial working class** and **Indian capitalists** (Tatas, Birlas)
- **Caste:** railways, schools, courts and jobs open to all weakened ritual distance
  - The **Census** (first all-India count 1872, first synchronous **1881**) recorded caste; **H.H. Risley (1901)** ranked castes by "social precedence", which made caste sharper and set off caste associations
  - Non-Brahmin and Depressed Class movements and reservations started (Communal Award 1932, Poona Pact)
- **Women:** girls' schools (Bethune School 1849), the first women graduates (Calcutta University 1883: Kadambini Ganguly, Chandramukhi Basu); women's bodies such as WIA (1917) and AIWC (1927)
- **Andhra angle:** **Veeresalingam** held the first Telugu **widow remarriage** at **Rajahmundry, 11 Dec 1881**; Raghupathi Venkataratnam Naidu led the **anti-nautch** (devadasi) campaign
  - **Madras Devadasis (Prevention of Dedication) Act, 1947**, pushed by **Muthulakshmi Reddy**
  - The Ryotwari system in Madras Presidency made the ryot a direct taxpayer
> Exam angle: British social laws followed Indian reformers' campaigns (Roy, Vidyasagar, Malabari). After 1857 the Queen's Proclamation promised **non-interference** in religion, so reform slowed. Traps: Sarda Act = 1929, not 1891; Caste Disabilities Act = Dalhousie 1850.
~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India (social-reform acts); NCERT Modern India (Bipan Chandra); Drishti IAS social reforms; census history (censusindia.gov.in)

add.title: Cultural Changes under British Rule – Orientalism, Literature, Theatre and Art
add.md:
# Cultural Changes under British Rule
- **Orientalism, i.e. the rediscovery of India's past:** **Asiatic Society of Bengal (1784, William Jones)**
  - **Charles Wilkins** translated the Gita into English (1785); Jones translated **Abhijnana Shakuntalam** (1789)
  - **Max Müller** edited the *Sacred Books of the East*; **James Prinsep** deciphered Brahmi (1837)
  - **ASI (1861, Alexander Cunningham)**; **Ancient Monuments Preservation Act, 1904 (Curzon)**
- **Printing revolution:** the **Serampore Mission Press (1800, William Carey)** printed Bibles and grammars in Bengali, Telugu and other languages
  - Cheap print spread newspapers, tracts and modern prose, so ideas reached more than a narrow elite
- **Modern Indian literature:** prose, the **novel** and the short story grew up
  - Bankim Chandra's *Durgeshnandini* (1865) and *Anandamath* (1882, *Vande Mataram*); Tagore's *Gitanjali*, the **Nobel Prize in 1913** (first Asian winner)
  - Telugu: **Veeresalingam**'s *Rajasekhara Charitramu* (1878), the first Telugu novel; **Gurajada**'s *Kanyasulkam* (staged 1892), a play in spoken Telugu
  - **Gidugu Ramamurthy** led the **vyavaharika (spoken-language) movement**
- **Theatre:** proscenium-stage drama in Bengali, Marathi, Parsi and Telugu
  - **Nil Darpan (1860, Dinabandhu Mitra)** on indigo planters; the British passed the **Dramatic Performances Act, 1876 (Northbrook)** to censor nationalist plays
  - Andhra: **Dharmavaram Ramakrishnamacharyulu**, called *Andhra Nataka Pitamaha*, founded **Sarasa Vinodini Sabha** (Bellary, c. 1886)
  - Also in Andhra: **Kolachalam Srinivasa Rao**; **Surabhi** family theatre (1885, Kadapa district)
- **Art:**
  - British art schools: Madras (1850), Calcutta (1854) and **Sir J.J. School, Bombay (1857)**
  - **Raja Ravi Varma** (1848-1906, Kilimanoor) used oil painting and set up a **lithograph press** (Bombay, 1894; later Malavli) that made images of the gods cheap for everyone
  - Reaction: the **Bengal School**, led by **Abanindranath Tagore** (*Bharat Mata*, 1905) with **E.B. Havell**, and the **Indian Society of Oriental Art (1907)**, revived Indian styles in the Swadeshi era
- **Architecture:** the **Indo-Saracenic** style, for example Madras High Court and Chennai Central; **Victoria Memorial (1921)**; **New Delhi** by **Lutyens and Baker** (inaugurated 1931)
- **Ideas:** rationalism, humanism and the use of the past as a source of pride together led to the **Indian Renaissance** and fed cultural nationalism
> Exam angle: British rule had two cultural effects. Westernisation came through English education and print. Indians reacted by reviving their own heritage (the Orientalists, the Bengal School, *Vande Mataram*). The Dramatic Performances Act (1876) came two years before the Vernacular Press Act (1878).
~~ Sources: Spectrum Modern India (education, press, culture); NCERT Modern India; Wikipedia: Dharmavaram Ramakrishnamacharyulu, Raja Ravi Varma; Google Arts & Culture (Ravi Varma Press); livehistoryindia.com
